title: Compass and Clock
premise: In 1899, apprentice clockmaker Wendell Eriksen is summoned to the coastal observatory of Vesterhavn to repair its failing master clock, a machine whose accuracy governs every ship's departure. There he finds an abandoned infant left with a note instructing him to forget the face, and he realizes the child is entangled in his own family's hidden past: his estranged uncle, the observatory's dying keeper, has been hiding evidence that Wendell's father, long believed lost at sea, defected with smuggled inheritance papers meant for another branch of the family. As the century turns, Wendell must repair both clock and family, choosing which relative—his ambitious sister Astrid or the child—receives the last berth on the ship leaving before the new year. He gives the berth to the child, stays to claim his own name publicly, and lets the master clock chime midnight over a family rebuilt rather than escaped.
about_author: Bram Dunmore is the pen name of a former maritime museum archivist who spent a decade cataloguing lighthouse logs and horological ledgers along the North Sea coast. Compass and Clock is their second novel, following a well-received debut about a cartographer who maps a town that no longer exists.

chapters.title: The Weight of Small Gears
chapters.summary: Wendell Eriksen, POV. In his cramped workshop, Wendell measures his life in portable things: tools, a photograph, debts. The summons from Vesterhavn Observatory arrives, offering wages he cannot refuse. Emotional beat: restless ambition shadowed by the fear that leaving means disappearing like his father did.

chapters.title: A Summons in Brass
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. He travels north by coastal steamer, rehearsing deference for the observatory's keeper. A fellow passenger warns that Vesterhavn keeps its own time and its own secrets. Emotional beat: anticipation curdling into unease as the observatory's tower rises from the fog.

chapters.title: The Keeper Who Counts Backward
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. He meets Uncle Halvard Eriksen, the observatory keeper, who recognizes him instantly but pretends otherwise. The master clock is sabotaged, not merely broken—a gear deliberately filed. Emotional beat: cold courtesy masking recognition and old guilt.

chapters.title: What the Tide Left
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. At dawn, a wicker basket appears at the observatory door: an infant, wrapped in wool embroidered with the Eriksen crest, and a note reading 'forget the face.' Emotional beat: shock hardening into reluctant responsibility.

chapters.title: The Housekeeper's Silence
chapters.summary: Maren, the housekeeper, POV. Maren agrees to nurse the child but refuses to say where she learned the crest's meaning. She burns the note when Wendell isn't looking. Emotional beat: loyalty divided between kindness and a promise made years ago.

chapters.title: Teeth of the Escapement
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. Repairing the clock, Wendell finds a hollowed gear containing a folded document: shipping manifests and an inheritance deed naming his father. He hides it. Emotional beat: the thrill of discovery tangled with dread about what his father actually did.

chapters.title: Astrid Arrives
chapters.summary: Astrid, Wendell's sister, POV. Summoned by an anonymous letter, Astrid arrives sharp-tongued and calculating, claiming the deed proves their family was robbed by Halvard's line. She begins courting the harbor magistrate. Emotional beat: love for her brother weaponized into ambition.

chapters.title: The Child Who Won't Sleep
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. Nights of pacing with the crying infant between clock repairs; the baby quiets only to the tick of the master clock. Wendell names her Ilsa without deciding to. Emotional beat: tenderness arriving uninvited, softening his armor.

chapters.title: Halvard's Confession, Half-Told
chapters.summary: Halvard, POV. Dying of a weak heart, Halvard tells Wendell fragments: his father didn't drown—he took the deed and ran, and Halvard let the sea be blamed. He begs Wendell to burn the documents. Emotional beat: shame finally surfacing after thirty years.

chapters.title: The Magistrate's Interest
chapters.summary: Astrid, POV. Astrid shows the magistrate the deed, positioning herself as heir to reclaim property and status. He warns her that inheritance claims invite scrutiny of how the deed left the family. Emotional beat: triumph shadowed by the first flicker of doubt.

chapters.title: Storm Glass Falling
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. A winter storm strands ships in harbor; the observatory's time signal becomes critical for departures. The clock fails again—sabotage repeated—and suspicion falls on Wendell himself. Emotional beat: isolation deepening as the town turns wary.

chapters.title: Maren Breaks Her Promise
chapters.summary: Maren, POV. Pressured by Astrid, Maren admits she once served the other branch of the family and delivered the baby at Astrid's instruction—Astrid knew of Ilsa all along. Emotional beat: guilt transmuted into quiet defiance.

chapters.title: Two Names on One Deed
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. Wendell confronts Astrid; she argues the child is leverage, not family, and that the berth on the departing ship—the last before the year ends—is theirs to sell. Emotional beat: sibling love cracking under competing claims of duty.

chapters.title: The Clockmaker's Ledger
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. Searching Halvard's records, Wendell learns his father wrote letters from abroad—alive, perhaps still alive—and that Halvard answered them all. Emotional beat: grief for a living man, fury at decades of silence.

chapters.title: Midnight Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Maren, POV. The household prepares for New Year's Eve, when the repaired clock will signal the century's turn and the ship will sail with the tide. Maren sews Ilsa a traveling coat, pretending it's for warmth, not farewell. Emotional beat: foreboding stitched into domestic routine.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Harbor Office
chapters.summary: Astrid, POV. Astrid sells information about the deed to the magistrate to secure her claim, inadvertently triggering an inquiry that could take Ilsa into parish custody. Emotional beat: victory tasting of ash as she realizes what she's traded.

chapters.title: The Choice Before the Chime
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. With one berth, one ship, and hours remaining, Wendell weighs sending Ilsa away to safety against keeping her and facing the inquiry together. Halvard, failing fast, urges him to send the child and save the name. Emotional beat: the novel's moral fulcrum—love against duty made literal.

chapters.title: Sabotage Confessed
chapters.summary: Maren, POV. Maren reveals she filed the gears—not to destroy the clock, but to delay departures until the truth could surface, acting on a letter from Wendell's father asking her to watch over Halvard's conscience. Emotional beat: revelation reframing every earlier suspicion.

chapters.title: The Last Berth
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. At the dock, Wendell places Ilsa in the arms of a trustworthy widow sailing to relatives abroad, giving up the berth he might have used to flee the inquiry himself. Emotional beat: heartbreak chosen freely—the cost of staying visible.

chapters.title: When the Century Turns
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. Wendell starts the master clock by hand; its midnight chime rolls over the harbor as the ship vanishes into dark water. He publicly signs the observatory ledger 'Wendell Eriksen, clockmaker,' claiming his name before the magistrate. Emotional beat: exaltation braided with loss.

chapters.title: Reckoning in the Tower Room
chapters.summary: Astrid, POV. Confronted with Maren's testimony and Halvard's written confession, Astrid's claim collapses—but Wendell offers her a share of the restored inheritance if she helps raise Ilsa when the widow writes back. Emotional beat: pride breaking open into the possibility of forgiveness.

chapters.title: Time Kept, Time Given
chapters.summary: Wendell, POV. Spring: Halvard dies at peace; a letter arrives from the widow with news of Ilsa, and a second letter postmarked from abroad bears Wendell's father's handwriting. Wendell winds the clock and leaves the tower door unlocked. Emotional beat: resolution as continuation—an inheritance redefined as people kept, not property claimed.
